nodes.label: Indra and Virocana
nodes.sub: Two students hear Prajāpati's first answer. Virocana leaves satisfied and teaches it to his people; Indra sees the flaw, returns three times, and is taught the truth after a hundred and one years.

nodes.label: Satyakāma tells the truth
nodes.sub: Asked his lineage, a boy repeats his mother's honest answer that she does not know it. The teacher accepts him because he did not swerve from the truth.

nodes.label: Śvetaketu's pride

nodes.label: Nārada knows the texts

nodes.label: Maitreyī's question

nodes.label: Bhṛgu learns by inquiry
nodes.sub: Bhṛgu asks his father for Brahman. Varuṇa gives him clues and sends him to find out. Five times Bhṛgu returns with a deeper answer, until he reaches bliss.

nodes.label: The gods and the Yakṣa
nodes.sub: The gods take a victory for their own. A mysterious being sets a blade of grass before Agni and Vāyu, who cannot burn or move it. Umā tells Indra who it was.

nodes.label: Sukeśa will not lie

edges.why: Names the good and the pleasant as two different ends that bind a person differently.
The steady one examines both and chooses the good over the pleasant.
Yama praises Naciketas for refusing every pleasant offer.
Kaṭha sets the two side by side: one leads to the good, the other falls short of the goal.
The pleasant is the second of the two roads.
The dull choose the pleasant for the sake of getting and keeping.
Yama offers long life, sons and wealth to turn Naciketas from his question.
Naciketas: these pleasures last till tomorrow and wear out the vigour of the senses.
'Examining both, the steady one separates them' (samparītya vivinakti).
With discernment the mind is held steady and the senses obey, like good horses.
Having examined the worlds won by works, the seeker turns away from them.
Truth alone triumphs, not untruth; by truth the path to the divine is laid.
The face of truth is hidden by a golden vessel; the seeker asks for it to be uncovered.
The teacher's parting instruction begins: speak the truth.
Gautama accepts Satyakāma because he did not swerve from the truth about himself.
Satyam eva jayate, nānṛtam: truth wins, untruth does not.
Sukeśa would rather say 'I do not know' than speak untruth, which withers a person to the root.
Untruth does not triumph.
Knowledge and ignorance lead far apart; Naciketas desires knowledge.
Crossing death by the one, one attains immortality by the other.
'Widely opposed and leading to different ends are these two: ignorance and what is known as knowledge.'
Ignorance is the opposite road to knowledge.
Living in ignorance yet thinking themselves wise, they wander like the blind led by the blind.
The same verse, repeated in the Muṇḍaka.
Those who worship ignorance enter blinding darkness.
Two kinds of knowledge are to be known, the higher and the lower.
The higher is that by which the imperishable is attained.
The Muṇḍaka opens its teaching with this division.
The four Vedas and the six auxiliary sciences are counted as the lower knowledge.
Nārada has mastered every science, yet says: 'I know only the texts, not the Self.'
The Self is not attained by discourse, intellect or much learning.
'If you think you know it well, you surely know very little.'
'I do not think I know it well, nor that I do not know it.'
'It is not understood by those who understand; it is understood by those who do not.'
The gods thought, 'This victory is ours, this glory is ours.'
Śvetaketu returns from study conceited, thinking himself learned, and stiff.
Thinking 'I know it well' is the mark of knowing little.
Know the self as the rider, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer, the mind as the reins.
One whose charioteer is discernment and who holds the reins of the mind reaches the end of the road.
The senses are the horses; their objects are the roads they run on.
Without discernment, the senses are like vicious horses.
The senses were made outward-turning, so one looks outward, not within.
A rare steady person, desiring immortality, turned the eye inward and saw the inner self.
The childish follow outward desires into the wide net of death.
The knowing Self is not born and does not die.
This Self is Brahman; it has four quarters.
One who sees all beings in the Self, and the Self in all, does not recoil from anyone.
'All this is Brahman. This Self is Brahman.'
What speech cannot express but by which speech is expressed: know that to be Brahman.
'Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite.'
Approach, fuel in hand, a teacher learned in the Veda and established in Brahman.
Taught by an inferior person, it is not well understood.
Bhṛgu asks his father to teach him Brahman; he is given clues and told to seek, and he undertakes tapas.
Bhṛgu reaches a first answer, returns, and is told again: seek to know Brahman by tapas.
Every virtue is listed together with 'study and teaching'.
'Do not neglect your own study.'
To the gods, Da means 'restrain yourselves'.
To humans, Da means 'give'.
To the demons, Da means 'be compassionate'; the thunder repeats it.
A person is made of desire; desire becomes will, will becomes deed, deed becomes destiny.
When all desires lodged in the heart fall away, the mortal becomes immortal.
The childish run after outward desires.
'The boundless is joy; there is no joy in the small.'
Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else: that is the boundless.
The other bird, not eating, looks on.
When the grieving bird sees the other, the Lord, its sorrow ends.
Two birds, companions on one tree: one eats the sweet fruit, the other looks on.
One bird eats the sweet fruit.
Sunk on the same tree, the person grieves, deluded by helplessness.
The Fourth is neither inward- nor outward-knowing; it is the Self, to be known.
The partless OM is the Fourth.
Virocana left Prajāpati 'satisfied in his heart', carrying a wrong teaching. Satisfaction was not understanding.
Thinking themselves wise, they wander like the blind led by the blind.
A golden lid can cover the face of truth.

The 'blind leading the blind' verse appears almost word for word in both Upanishads.
